'''''Rubus spectabilis''''', the '''salmonberry''', is a species of [[bramble]] native to the west coast of North America. Its fruit is typically yellow-orange or red, resembling [[raspberry|raspberries]]. The plant grows in the wild, and is not cultivated.

==Distribution==
The plant is native to the west coast of North America from west-central [[Alaska]] to [[California]], and inland as far as [[Idaho]].<ref name="zouhar-2019"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.calflora.org/cgi-bin/species_query.cgi?where-calrecnum=7203|title=''Rubus spectabilis'' {{small|Pursh}} |publisher=Calflora taxon report, The Calflora Database|date=2026|access-date=5 August 2026}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Rubus spectabilis'' is a [[deciduous]], [[rhizomatous]] shrub growing to {{convert|1-4|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} tall and 9 m (30 ft) wide, with a moderate growth rate of {{Convert|0.3–0.6|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} per year.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Salmon Berry, Rubus spectabilis |url=https://calscape.org/Rubus-spectabilis-() |access-date=2022-10-22 |website=calscape.org}}</ref> 30–40% of the plant's biomass is underground.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tappeiner |first1=John |last2=Zasada |first2=John |last3=Ryan |first3=Peter |last4=Newton |first4=Michael |date=April 1991 |title=Salmonberry Clonal and Population Structure: The Basis for a Persistent Cover |journal=Ecology |volume=72 |issue=2 |pages=609–618 |doi=10.2307/2937201 |jstor=2937201 |bibcode=1991Ecol...72..609T |issn=0012-9658}}</ref> It has [[perennial]] (not [[Biennial plant|biennial]]) woody stems that are covered with fine [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|prickles]], especially on new growth.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web|title=USDA Plants Database |url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=RUSP |access-date=2021-12-05|website=plants.usda.gov}}</ref> The plant has golden or yellowish brown erect or arching stems (also known as "canes") that often form thickets, like many other [[bramble]]s.

The [[leaves]] are alternate, trifoliate (with three leaflets), {{convert|7-22|cm|in|abbr=off|frac=2}} long and typically ovate in shape, with the terminal leaflet being larger than the two side leaflets, which are sometimes shallowly lobed. The margins of the leaflets are [[doubly serrate]].<ref name="whitney-1985">{{cite book|last=Whitney|first=Stephen |url=https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit |title=Western Forests (The Audubon Society Nature Guides) |date=1985 |publisher=Knopf|isbn=978-0-394-73127-8|page=[https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/419 419]|location=New York}}</ref><ref name="pbc3">{{cite web |title=Plants of British Columbia: ''Rubus spectabilis'' |url=http://linnet.geog.ubc.ca/Atlas/Atlas.aspx?sciname=Rubus+spectabilis |access-date=December 9, 2014 |publisher=Linnet.geog.ubc.ca |archive-date=March 14, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170314112407/http://linnet.geog.ubc.ca/Atlas/Atlas.aspx?sciname=Rubus+spectabilis }}</ref> The leaves are also stipulate and are smooth to slightly hairy on the top surface, compared to the underside, which are typically more pale and hairy.<ref name="pbc3" /> In late fall and winter months, salmonberry leaves will fall, and the plant remains dormant or maintains minimal shoot elongation during the winter.<ref name="zouhar-2019">{{Cite web |title=''Rubus spectabilis''|last=Zouhar |first=Kris |publisher= Fire Effects Information System, US Department of Agriculture|date=2019|url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/shrub/rubspe/all.html |access-date=2022-10-22}}</ref>

The flowers are {{convert|2-3|cm|frac=4|abbr=on}} in diameter, with a calyx of five hairy [[sepal]]s and five pinkish-purple petals that surround a cluster of stamens; they are produced between April and July, either singly or in clusters of 2 or 3. The flowers are [[Plant reproductive morphology|perfect (bisexual)]], containing 75–100 stamens and many individual pistils with superior ovaries.<ref name="whitney-1985" /><ref name="pbc3" /> While fruit production is largely dependent on the environment, there is an estimated growth of 30 fruits per {{Convert|3|m2}} and 17–65 seeds per fruit.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Sastry |first1=K. Subramanya |title=Rubus spp. (Blackberry, Blackraspberry, Caneberry, Raspberry, Redraspberry, Wineberry) |date=2019 |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Plant Viruses and Viroids |pages=2111–2133 |place=New Delhi |publisher=Springer India |last2=Mandal |first2=Bikash |last3=Hammond |first3=John |last4=Scott |first4=S. W. |last5=Briddon |first5=R. W.|doi=10.1007/978-81-322-3912-3_805 |isbn=978-81-322-3911-6 |s2cid=239272713 }}</ref> Salmonberry sprout mainly from the buds found on rhizomes, stumps, and root crowns of the plant. The flowers cannot [[self-pollinate]] and are instead pollinated by insects, hummingbirds, and beetles.<ref name="zouhar-2019" />

Salmonberries ripen approximately 30–36 days after pollination, from early May to late July in most of the [[Pacific Northwest]] and July to August in cooler Northern climates. They are {{convert|1.5-2|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} long and resemble large shiny yellow to dark-red [[raspberries]]. The fruit pulls away from its [[Receptacle (botany)|receptacle]], differentiating it from [[blackberries]].{{citation needed|date=August 2022}} Botanically speaking, the salmonberry is not a true [[Berry (botany)|berry]], but instead an [[aggregate fruit]] made of many smaller [[drupe]]lets.<ref name="pbc3" /><ref name="jeps2">{{cite web|title=Jepson Flora: ''Rubus spectabilis''|url=http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?Rubus+spectabilis|access-date=December 9, 2014|publisher=Ucjeps.berkeley.edu}}</ref> 

=== Fruit polymorphism ===
{{Multiple image
| image1            = Salmonberry, Carson, WA 98610, USA imported from iNaturalist photo 525947271 (cropped).jpg
| image2            = Salmonberry, Lane County, OR, USA imported from iNaturalist photo 686872353 (cropped).jpg
| align             = right
| total_width       = 260
| caption1          = Red morph
| caption2          = Yellow morph
}}
Salmonberry fruits are [[Polymorphism (biology)|polymorphic]]; different plants will produce berries that are either red in color or a yellow-orange color. Studies have found that although both red and yellow-orange morphs have similar physical qualities, the red berries are more commonly consumed by birds, although this is likely not a strong enough [[selective pressure]] to determine color morph distribution alone; factors such as soil type (which affects germination), along with other unstudied factors are more likely responsible for the color polymorphism.<ref name="ubc3">{{cite web|last=Mosquin|first=Daniel|date=2026|title=''Rubus spectabilis'' |publisher=University of British Columbia Botanical Garden |url=https://ubc.gardenexplorer.org/taxon-17124.aspx|access-date=5 August 2026}}</ref><ref name="Traveset">{{Cite journal|last1=Traveset|first1=Anna |last2=Willson|first2=Mary F.|date=March 1998|title=Ecology of the fruit-colour polymorphism in Rubus spectabilis |journal=Evolutionary Ecology|volume=12|issue=3 |pages=331–345|doi=10.1023/A:1006504317585 |bibcode=1998EvEco..12..331T |s2cid=41661194 |issn=1573-8477}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gervais |first1=Jennifer A.|last2=Noon|first2=B.|last3=Willson |first3=M.|date=1999|title=Avian selection of the color-dimorphic fruits of salmonberry, Rubus spectabilis: a field experiment |journal=Oikos |volume=84 |issue=1 |pages=77–86 |doi=10.2307/3546868 |jstor=3546868 |bibcode=1999Oikos..84...77G |s2cid=87682589 }}</ref> The orange morph is more common at lower latitudes such as Oregon, while the red morph is more common at higher latitudes. The yellow morph is more resistant to desiccation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Burns |first=Kevin C. |date=2015-10-26 |title=The color of plant reproduction: macroecological trade-offs between biotic signaling and abiotic tolerance |journal=Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution |language=English |volume=3 |page=118 |doi=10.3389/fevo.2015.00118 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2015FrEEv...3..118B |issn=2296-701X}}</ref>
===Similar species===
A similar species from Japan, the red-flowered raspberry, was once considered a [[subspecies]] as ''R. spectabilis'' subsp. ''vernus'', although it is now reclassified as a distinct species ''[[Rubus vernus|R. vernus]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Naruhashi |first=Naruhito |date=June 15, 1980|title=Rubus vernus FOCKE and R. spectabilis PURSH|url=https://kanazawa-u.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=repository_action_common_download&item_id=50069&item_no=1&attribute_id=26&file_no=1|journal=The Journal of Phytogeography and Taxonomy (The Journal of Geobotany)|volume=28|page=13|via=ISSN 0388-6212}}</ref>

==Habitat==
[[File:Salmonberry, Baring, WA 98224, USA imported from iNaturalist photo 518813005.jpg|thumb|Leaves, in [[Washington (state)|Washington]]]]
Salmonberries are typically found in coastal areas with [[Nitrophily|nitrogen-rich soils]], in moist to wet forests and streambanks, increasing in abundance in areas of high rainfall and decreasing in abundance at higher elevations and continentality. Ecologically speaking, salmonberry tends to spread quickly and needs plenty of room to grow, and is often dominant and fast-growing in early-seral communities. Its size and population growth decline in abundance as the canopy begins to form, and may also be influenced by other factors such as basal area, plant disturbance, and population density.<ref name="pbc3" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Rubus spectabilis|url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/shrub/rubspe/all.html|access-date=2021-12-06|website=www.fs.fed.us}}</ref> In open areas they often form large thickets, and are found to associate with stands of red alder (''[[Alnus rubra]]''), lady fern (''[[Athyrium filix-femina|Athyrium filixfemina]]''), western skunk cabbage (''[[Lysichiton americanus]]''), devil's club (''[[Oplopanax horridus]]''), thimbleberry (''[[Rubus parviflorus]]''), and threeleaf foamflower (''[[Tiarella trifoliata]]'').<ref name="pbc3" />

==Ecology==
In the wild, the fruit are typically eaten by birds, bears, and small mammals, among others, while the leaves, twigs, and stems are grazed on by herbivores such as deer, moose, mountain goats, elk, and rabbits.<ref name="whitney-1985" /><ref name=":02" /> Populations of dense thicket growth can provide escape habitats for small animals, as well as nesting sites for birds.<ref name=":02" />[[File:Anna's Hummingbird, West Side, Vancouver, BC, Canada imported from iNaturalist photo 373708241.jpg|thumb|[[Anna's hummingbird]] feeding from salmonberry blossoms, in [[Vancouver]]]]In the spring, salmonberry flowering coincides with the migration of certain species of hummingbirds, which is crucial for its pollination.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pojar |first=Jim |date=1974-08-01 |title=Reproductive dynamics of four plant communities of southwestern British Columbia |journal=Canadian Journal of Botany |volume=52 |issue=8 |pages=1819–1834 |doi=10.1139/b74-234 |bibcode=1974CaJB...52.1819P |issn=0008-4026}}</ref> Birds and mammals also help with dispersion of seeds through their feces, while rodents and other burrowing animals may further help with dispersion. Some notable mammals crucial for the dispersion of seeds are the grizzly and American black bears, which can deposit 50,000 to 100,000 seeds in one pile of feces.<ref name=Traveset/>

Salmonberry have several traits that make it highly resistant to fire. Rhizomes and root crowns below the soil surface usually survive, even if top stems are burned. Depending on burial depth, seeds also often remain unharmed. Additionally, the plant tend to quickly sprout after fires, allowing for rapid growth and regeneration.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Oleskevich |first1=Carmen |last2=Punja |first2=Zamir K. |last3=Shamoun |first3=Simon F. |date=1996-01-01 |title=The biology of Canadian weeds. 105. ''Rubus strigosus'' Michx., ''Rubus parviflorus'' Nutt., and ''Rubus spectabilis'' Pursh. |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |volume=76 |issue=1 |pages=187–201 |doi=10.4141/cjps96-037 |issn=0008-4220|doi-access=free |bibcode=1996CJPlS..76..187O }}</ref>

Salmonberries are susceptible to many diseases, including mildew, fruit rot, rust, root rot, and viral and bacterial diseases. Their fruits, foliage, canes, roots, and crowns may also be damaged by pests such as beetles, aphids, mites, moths, among others.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=G. |first1=R. V. |last2=Ellis |first2=Michael A. |last3=Converse |first3=Richard H. |last4=Williams |first4=Roger N. |last5=Williamson |first5=Brian |date=November 1992 |title=Compendium of Raspberry and Blackberry Diseases and Insects |journal=Mycologia |volume=84 |issue=6 |page=953 |doi=10.2307/3760307 |jstor=3760307 |issn=0027-5514}}</ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Bowl of salmonberries.jpg|thumb|200px|Colander of salmonberries]]

Salmonberries are edible plants.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Fagan |first=Damian|title=Wildflowers of Oregon: A Field Guide to Over 400 Wildflowers, Trees, and Shrubs of the Coast, Cascades, and High Desert|publisher=[[FalconGuides]] |year=2019|isbn=978-1-4930-3633-2|location=Guilford, CT |page=222|oclc=1073035766}}</ref><ref name="ubc3"/> One field guide refers to the fruit as "diverse, from bright, fruity and citrusy to deep and earthy with spicy notes".<ref name="deur2014">{{cite book|last=Deur|first=Douglas|date=2014|title=Pacific Northwest Foraging: 120 Wild and Flavorful Edibles from Alaska Blueberries to Wild Hazelnuts|publisher=Timber Press|isbn=978-1-60469-352-2|page=175}}</ref> Depending on ripeness and site, they are good eaten raw {{ndash}} whether red or golden<ref name="ubc3" /> {{ndash}} and processed into jam, candy, jelly and wine.

Native American people ate the young [[Shoot (botany)|shoot]]s or used it as a medicinal plant. The shoots were harvested during April to early June before they turned woody or tough, and were peeled, then steamed, boiled, or [[Earth oven|pit-cooked]], and eaten (or less commonly, eaten raw).<ref name=":02" /><ref>{{cite book|last=Lyons |first=C. P.|title=Trees, Shrubs and Flowers to Know in Washington|date=1956|publisher=J. M. Dent & Sons |edition=1st|location=Canada|page=88|author-link=C. P. Lyons}}</ref> Traditionally, the berries and sprouts were also eaten with salmon or mixed with [[Eulachon|oolichan]] grease or salmon roe. They were not dried because of their high moisture content.<ref name=":02" /><ref name="Pojar2">{{cite book|last1=Pojar|first1=Jim|title=Plants Of The Pacific Northwest Coast: Washington, Oregon, British Columbia & Alaska|first2=Andy|last2=MacKinnon|date=2004 |publisher=Lone Pine Publishing|isbn=978-1-55105-530-5 |page=76}}</ref> It is still used as a food source and medicinal plant in regions of Alaska today.

Other uses by Native Americans include:<ref name=":02"/>

* Boiling the leaves with fish as a flavoring (by the [[Nuu-chah-nulth people|''Nuu-chah-nulth'' people]])
* Using the leaves to line baskets, wipe fish, and cover cooking pits (by the [[Haida people|Kaigani Haida]] people)
* Using the branches as a [[Tobacco pipe|pipe stem]] (by the [[Makah people]])
* Chewing and spitting the leaves (or bark in the winter) onto a burn as a treatment due to their astringent qualities (by the [[Quileute people]])
* Boiling the bark in seawater to create a brew to clean infected wounds (especially burns) as well as reduce labor pains (by the [[Quinault people]])
[[File:Rubus spectabilis 'Olympic Double' - Hillier Gardens - Romsey, Hampshire, England - DSC04487.jpg|thumb|''R. spectabilis'' 'Olympic Double', a [[double-flowered]] ornamental cultivar]]
It is also widely grown as an [[ornamental plant]] for its flowers,<ref name="ubc3" /><ref>Mulligan, Brian O. (1977). ''Woody Plants in the University of Washington Arboretum, Washington Park''. University of Washington, College of Forest Resources, Seattle.</ref><ref>Mulligan, Brian O. (1963). Accession records of the University of Washington Arboretum</ref> with a double-flowered [[Clone (cell biology)|clone]] identified in [[Washington (state)|Washington]] and [[British Columbia]].<ref name="mosquin2">{{cite web|last=Mosquin|first=Daniel|date=23 April 2007|title=''Rubus spectabilis'' Double-Flowered Group|url=https://botanyphoto.botanicalgarden.ubc.ca/2007/04/rubus-spectabilis-double-flowered-group/|access-date=12 April 2021|publisher=University of British Columbia Botanical Garden}}</ref> ''R. spectabilis'' has [[Escaped plant|escaped cultivation]] and become [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in parts of northwestern Europe, including [[Great Britain]], [[Ireland]] and the [[Faroe Islands]].<ref name="fnwe2">{{cite web|author=Inland Fisheries Ireland|title=Risk Assessment of Rubus spectabilis|url=http://nonnativespecies.ie/wp-content/uploads/2014/03/Rubus-spectabilis-Salmonberry.pdf|access-date=May 1, 2018|website=nonnativespecies.ie|publisher=National Biodiversity Data Centre}}</ref><ref>Højgaard, A. et al., eds. (1989). ''A century of tree-planting in the Faroe Islands''. Føroya Fróðskaparfelag, Tórshavn.</ref>

== In culture ==
The salmonberry is important to multiple indigenous people of America in its native range. The [[Makah|Makah people]] call the plant ''ka'k'we'abupt'' and the berry ''ka'k'we''; the [[Cowlitz people]] call the plant ''e'twanac'' and the berry ''e'twan''; speakers of [[Lower Chinook]] call it ''yunts''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rubus spectabilis |website=Mount Pisgah Arboretum |url=https://mountpisgaharboretum.org/learn/plant-list/rubus-spectabilis/ |access-date=2023-04-08}}</ref> The [[Squamish people]] call the plant ''yetwánáy'' and the berries ''yetwán'', the shoots are called ''stsá7tskaý'' (pronounced ''saskay'').<ref name="joseph-2017" /> In the [[Saanich dialect]], it is called ''elile''.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://people.geog.uvic.ca/wanthony/website/geog490/NativePlantTable-1.htm | title=Native Plant Names - SENĆOŦEN & English }}</ref>

The birdsong of the [[Swainson's thrush]], sometimes known as the salmonberry bird, is believed by some indigenous people of the Pacific Northwest Coast to cause the ripening of salmonberries,<ref name="joseph-2017">{{Cite web |last=Joseph |first=Leigh |title=The Gifts of Yetwánaý (Salmon Berry) |url=https://leighjoseph.com/field-notes/the-gifts-of-yetwanay-salmon-berry|access-date=2026-06-25 |website=Leigh Joseph (Styawat), Ethnobotanist|date=24 April 2017 }}</ref> as is the case of the [[Saanich people]] who give the birdsong the [[Onomatopoeia|onomatopoeic]] translation of "''xwexwelexwelexwelexwesh!''" meaning "ripen, ripen, ripen, ripen!" This belief is also widespread and is known to the [[Tlingit]], [[Haida people|Haida]], [[Haisla people|Haisla]], [[Oweekeno]], [[Kwakwakaʼwakw|Kwakwaka'wakw]], Nuu-Chah-Nulth, [[Ditidaht First Nation|Ditidaht]], [[Sḵwx̱wú7mesh]], and the [[Straits Salish]] people. The presence of ''[[Elasmostethus cruciatus]]'', called the salmonberry bug, is also seen as an indicator to Northwest Coast indigenous peoples that salmonberry shoots are ready to harvest.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Turner |first1=Nancy J. |last2=Reid |first2=Andrea J. |date=2022-11-01 |title="When the Wild Roses Bloom": Indigenous Knowledge and Environmental Change in Northwestern North America |journal=GeoHealth |volume=6 |issue=11 |article-number=e2022GH000612 |issn=2471-1403 |doi=10.1029/2022GH000612|pmc=9665002|pmid=36398276|bibcode=2022GHeal...6..612T }}</ref>
